title: Spectral density of angular momentum transfer from a swift electron to a large spherical nanoparticle
abstract: Swift electrons in scanning transmission electron microscopy transfer both linear and angular momentum to nanoparticles, underlying electron-beam-driven nanoscale manipulation ("electron tweezers"). Prior theory relied either on the small-particle (dipolar) approximation, valid only well below experimentally relevant sizes, or on frequency-integrated multipolar calculations that leave the spectral structure of the interaction unresolved. Here we present a fully retarded, causal, multipole-converged electrodynamical methodology for the angular momentum transfer from a swift electron to an isolated spherical nanoparticle, based on a closed-surface Maxwell stress tensor formulation whose angular integrals reduce analytically to a small, material- and trajectory-independent set of irreducible integrals over associated Legendre functions. This lowers the cost of the double multipolar sum from O(l_max^4) to O(l_max^3), enabling convergence up to l_max=51 for nanoparticles as large as a=50 nm, nearly four times the order of the largest previous calculation at this size and previously unreached for an optically complex material, at three to four orders of magnitude lower cost. Applied to aluminum and gold nanoparticles up to a=50 nm, the method resolves the transfer's spectral density across the full frequency domain, showing it is set by interference between the electron and scattered fields, dominating at essentially every frequency; the electric contribution exceeds the magnetic one by two to three orders of magnitude, though spectral resolution reveals sign changes in the magnetic term hidden in the frequency-integrated transfer. At a=50 nm, gold transfers substantially more angular momentum than aluminum despite its more intricate response, by a factor growing with velocity from about 2x at v=0.5c to more than 6x as v->c (fixed b=51 nm from the nanoparticle center).
summary: This work develops a highly efficient, fully retarded electrodynamical method to calculate the spectral density of angular momentum transferred from a swift electron to a large spherical nanoparticle. By optimizing the multipole summation, the authors can analyze nanoparticles up to 50 nm, revealing that the transfer is governed by field interference and showing material-dependent enhancements in angular momentum transfer, particularly for gold.
main_problem: The paper determines the spectral density of angular momentum transfer ($\Delta L$) from a swift electron to a large spherical nanoparticle.
main_result: The method successfully calculates the full spectral density, showing the transfer is dominated by interference between the electron and scattered fields, and quantifies the enhanced angular momentum transfer in gold compared to aluminum as electron velocity increases.
method: It employs a fully retarded, causal, multipole-converged electrodynamical methodology based on the closed-surface Maxwell stress tensor formulation.
model_or_system: The system involves a spherical nanoparticle (radius $a$) characterized by a dielectric function $\epsilon(\omega)$, interacting with a swift electron traveling at velocity $v$ at an impact parameter $b$.
key_observables: Spectral density of angular momentum transfer, $L_n(\omega)$, and the ratio of electric to magnetic contributions.
important_parameters: Nanoparticle size ($a$ up to 50 nm), electron velocity ($v$), and impact parameter ($b$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to an isolated, local, spherical electrodynamic description, and the calculation relies on the closed-surface Maxwell stress tensor formulation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the setup: a spherical NP interacting with a swift electron via a closed-surface integral $S$. Figure 2 likely shows the frequency-resolved spectral density $|L|$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the electrodynamical theory using multipole expansions, derives the angular integrals in terms of irreducible integrals, and applies this optimized method to calculate the spectral density for various materials and parameters.
why_interesting: While focused on electron-matter interaction rather than quantum information, the rigorous development of a highly efficient, scalable electrodynamical calculation method (reducing complexity from $O(\ell^4)$ to $O(\ell^3)$) is a significant computational achievement applicable to complex open quantum system modeling.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematics of the system under study. A spheri- cal nanoparticle of radius a, characterized by a frequency- dependent dielectric function ϵ(ω), is embedded in vacuum and centered at the origin. A swift electron (blue dot) trav- els with constant velocity v = v ˆz at an impact parameter b relative to the NP center. The angular-momentum trans- fer is obtained from a closed-surface integral of the Maxwell stress tensor over the integration surface S (grey), a sphere of radius R satisfying a < R < b, so that it fully encloses the nanoparticle without intersecting the electron trajectory; one wedge of S facing the reader has been omitted purely for visual clarity.

FIG. 2. Frequency-resolved spectral density |L| in Log scale, decomposed into its electric (blue) and magnetic (red) contri- butions, each split into the interaction (solid) and scattered-scattered (dashed) terms of the Maxwell stress tensor [Eq. (2)]; the external-external term vanishes identically. a) Aluminum, a = 5 nm, b = 5.50 nm, v = 0.7c. b) Aluminum, a = 30 nm, b = 30.50 nm, v = 0.7c.

Total angular momentum transfer ∆L (thick line with markers), and its electric interaction (∆Lint E , thin solid blue), electric scattered-scattered (∆Lscat E , dashed blue), mag- netic interaction (∆Lint H , thin solid red, ×10), and magnetic scattered-scattered (∆Lscat H , dashed red, ×10) contributions, transferred by a swift electron to an aluminum NP as a func- tion of v, at fixed b = a + 1 nm: a) a = 5 nm, b = 6 nm; b) a = 20 nm, b = 21 nm; c) a = 50 nm, b = 51 nm.
